title: Primary postpartum haemorrhage on delivery suite
desc: This station involves a rapid focused history and examination of a woman bleeding heavily after birth, then interpreting her observations and blood results, leading the resuscitation and escalation of a primary postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony, and explaining the plan, disposition and safety netting to her.
stem: You are the junior doctor on delivery suite and the first doctor to arrive in room 1. The patient is a 24-year-old woman who gave birth vaginally less than an hour ago and is now bleeding heavily. The midwife is at the bedside with a nurse assistant. You are the team leader. Say your actions and requests aloud.
tasks: As team leader, take a rapid focused history from the midwife and the patient and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations on arrival and on reassessment, and her blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach as team leader, including what you do first and the calls you make, and explain the plan and safety netting to the patient (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You play the delivery suite midwife in room 1 and answer for the patient, a 24-year-old woman who is alert, frightened and talking in short sentences. Be brisk and answer only what is asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine. If the candidate starts giving treatment orders, say "Noted" and let them carry on; management is marked in Part 2.

Opening line (midwife): "She is bleeding heavily. I gave the oxytocin injection at the birth but it is not slowing down."

History (give only when asked):

  • Spontaneous vaginal birth at 39 weeks, 40 minutes ago, after a very quick labour of about 2 hours. The baby is well, in the cot beside her.
  • Oxytocin 10 units IM was given with the birth of the baby. The placenta came by controlled cord traction and has been checked: complete, with complete membranes.
  • Small perineal graze only, not sutured.
  • The bleeding became heavy soon after the placenta, with clots. About 1,000 mL so far by weighed pads, and still bleeding.
  • She has not passed urine since labour started.
  • She is not breastfeeding; she chose formula feeding.
  • Second baby (G2P2). Her first birth, 3 years ago, was a normal vaginal birth with no heavy bleeding.
  • This pregnancy was uncomplicated. Booking haemoglobin 124 g/L. No high blood pressure or pre-eclampsia.
  • No asthma, no heart disease, no bleeding disorder and no blood thinners. No allergies. Weight 68 kg.
  • Blood group A-positive on file, antibody screen negative.
  • She was booked for early discharge home today.

The patient (if the candidate speaks to her): "I feel dizzy and cold, and I'm so thirsty." She asks "Is this normal? Is my baby okay?" She settles a little with brief, calm explanation.
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Part 1 is a rapid history and examination; if the candidate starts treatment, the examiner acknowledges it, and it counts when the management is marked in Part 2. The reassessment in Part 2 is a snapshot 5 minutes after arrival and is the same whatever was started in Part 1 (anything ordered but not shown there, such as oxygen, was still being set up). A high-performing candidate takes the lead, assigns roles with a T-sheet, gets the key history quickly (precipitate labour, oxytocin given, complete placenta, full bladder, not breastfeeding, no hypertension or asthma, blood group on file), and examines A to E, the fundus, the bladder and the genital tract. In Part 2 they recognise the shock index of 1.35 rising to 1.56, interpret the fibrinogen and lactate correctly, name atony, and give their first actions in order: help, oxygen, access and bloods, fundal massage and catheter, uterotonics with routes, tranexamic acid within 3 hours, bimanual compression, and the MTP and theatre called by 1,500 mL with key-information calls to blood bank and the theatre manager. They then explain honestly why discharge is cancelled, with specific discharge criteria, warning signs and follow-up.

A borderline candidate manages tone and gives drugs but is slow to escalate, misses the full bladder or the contraindications, gives long handovers or rings reception, omits tranexamic acid or bimanual compression, or misreads the fibrinogen. Their explanation to the patient is brief and lacks specific safety netting. A poor candidate does not recognise shock, does not control the uterus or empty the bladder, does not escalate and does not speak to the patient.
explain:
Recognition

Primary PPH is blood loss of 500 mL or more after vaginal birth within 24 hours; loss over 1,000 mL or signs of shock is treated as major. Visual estimates under-read the true loss, so weigh pads and linen. A shock index (HR over systolic BP) above 1 signals significant haemodynamic compromise needing urgent escalation. Here the shock index is 135/100 = 1.35 on arrival and 140/90 = 1.56 on reassessment, with SpO2 falling to 91%: she is compromised and getting worse, and a BP of 60/40 would be near-arrest. Give high-flow oxygen by face mask (for example 15 L/min) as part of resuscitation, without waiting for the SpO2 to fall.

The rapid history and examination

The history establishes the birth and third stage, the blood loss so far, the bladder, feeding, previous births and the conditions that change drug choice (hypertension for ergometrine, asthma for carboprost) or bleeding risk (bleeding disorders, anticoagulants). The examination is A to E, the fundus, the bladder and the genital tract, with the placenta checked.

The 4 Ts

Tone is the commonest cause (about 70%). Here a precipitate labour, a full bladder and no breastfeeding (so no natural oxytocin release from suckling) all promote atony. Also exclude Trauma (perineum, vagina, cervix, uterine rupture or inversion), Tissue (retained placenta or membranes) and Thrombin (coagulopathy, which can be a consequence of the haemorrhage itself).

Investigations and interpretation

Send group and crossmatch, FBC, coagulation with fibrinogen, and a venous gas with lactate. Hb falls late, so Hb 96 g/L at this point badly underestimates the deficit: transfuse on the clinical picture and the ongoing loss, not on this number. Fibrinogen is the earliest useful marker of severity. It rises to about 4 to 6 g/L by term, so 2.3 g/L is already low for her even though it sits inside the non-pregnant range. A fibrinogen below 2 g/L predicts progression to severe PPH: keep it above 2 g/L with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate within the MTP, and repeat it (or use point-of-care viscoelastic testing where available) while bleeding continues. Her INR and platelets are normal, so there is no established coagulopathy yet; in atony it develops later, with ongoing loss and dilution, so give blood products early and limit crystalloid. Keep platelets above 50 and temperature at 36 °C or above. Lactate 5.2 mmol/L with base excess -9 confirms hypoperfusion.

Treatment and escalation

Call for help and resuscitate while treating the cause. Rub up the fundus and expel clots, and empty the bladder. Give uterotonics in sequence, checking contraindications. Typical doses (check the local protocol): a further oxytocin 5 units by slow IV injection, then an oxytocin infusion; ergometrine 250 micrograms IM or slow IV, avoided in hypertension, pre-eclampsia and heart disease; carboprost 250 micrograms IM, repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses (2 mg), avoided in asthma; misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually or 800 to 1,000 micrograms rectally. Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes as soon as possible and within 3 hours of birth (its benefit falls with every minute of delay), with a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours. Apply bimanual compression while arranging definitive care. Activate the massive transfusion protocol or call theatre by 1,500 mL at the latest; calling early has no penalty. Calls give key information only (for example "Primary PPH, A-positive, MTP, delivery suite room 1") and theatre requests go to the theatre manager, not reception. A T-sheet tracks drugs, timing and cumulative loss.

Communication, disposition and safety netting

Stay at the bedside and give brief reassurance during cannulation and fundal checks, and answer her questions honestly. The planned early discharge is cancelled. She stays on monitored observations and may be considered for discharge once bleeding has settled, the uterus is firm, pulse is under 100, systolic BP is above 100 mmHg without postural symptoms, she is passing urine, Hb is rechecked with an iron plan, and VTE risk is reviewed. She should call 000 or come straight back for soaking more than one pad an hour, clots larger than a golf ball, fever of 38 °C or above, offensive lochia, dizziness or fainting, palpitations or breathlessness, or calf pain or swelling. Follow-up includes FBC and ferritin, GP and midwife review, a debrief, and a plan for birth in a hospital with transfusion capability in any future pregnancy.
points: Primary PPH is 500 mL or more after vaginal birth; tone causes most cases and risk factors here are precipitate labour, a full bladder and no breastfeeding.
A shock index above 1 signals significant haemodynamic compromise needing urgent escalation; BP 60/40 is near-arrest.
In major PPH with shock, give high-flow oxygen by face mask straight away; do not wait for the SpO2 to fall.
Work through the 4 Ts: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin.
Fundal massage, emptying the bladder and uterotonics (oxytocin IM and IV, ergometrine IM, carboprost IM, misoprostol, all per local protocol) treat tone.
Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes as soon as possible and within 3 hours of birth, with a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene and PPE; introduces self as team leader and allocates roles, including a scribe using a T-sheet to track drugs, times and cumulative blood loss.
Stays calm, uses closed-loop instructions, and gives the patient brief plain-language reassurance while working.
History
Takes a rapid focused history from the midwife:

kids.x: Time and mode of birth, and the precipitate labour of about 2 hours
Third stage: oxytocin IM given, placenta and membranes complete
Perineal trauma, when the heavy bleeding started and the blood loss so far
Bladder: has not passed urine since labour started

check.x: Asks about conditions that change drug choice or bleeding risk: hypertension or pre-eclampsia, asthma, heart disease, bleeding disorders, anticoagulants and allergies.
Asks about previous births and heavy bleeding, the booking haemoglobin and the blood group on file [A-positive].
Asks the patient how she feels [dizzy, cold and thirsty] and recognises these as symptoms of shock.
Examination
Performs a rapid A to E assessment:

kids.x: Airway, breathing and SpO2 [RR 26, chest clear, SpO2 95% on room air]
Circulation: pulse, BP, capillary refill and peripheries [HR 135, BP 100/60, CRT 4 seconds, cool and clammy]
Disability and glucose [alert, GCS 15, BGL 5.6 mmol/L]
Temperature and exposure [36.4 °C], keeping her warm

check.x: Palpates the fundus [soft, boggy, above the umbilicus] and finds a full bladder.
Inspects the perineum, vagina and cervix [small graze only, no tear or haematoma] and confirms the placenta and membranes are complete.
Interpretation
Calculates the shock index on arrival (HR 135 over systolic BP 100 = 1.35, above 1) and recognises significant haemodynamic compromise needing urgent escalation.
Recognises on reassessment a major PPH with worsening shock: 1,500 mL lost, HR 140, BP 90/50 (shock index 1.56) and SpO2 91% on room air.
Hb 96 g/L (booking 124) understates the acute loss, because haemoglobin falls late: transfusion is guided by the clinical picture and the ongoing loss, not this number.

Fibrinogen 2.3 g/L is low for term (usually 4 to 6) and is the early marker of severe PPH: keeps it above 2 g/L with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate within the MTP and repeats it; the normal INR and platelets show no established coagulopathy yet.
Lactate 5.2 mmol/L and base excess -9 show hypoperfusion; repeats them to guide resuscitation.
Names uterine atony (Tone) as the most likely cause, with precipitate labour, a full bladder and no breastfeeding as risk factors, and works through Trauma, Tissue and Thrombin.
Management
First, resuscitates while treating the cause:

kids.x: Calls the obstetric registrar or consultant and the anaesthetist
High-flow oxygen by face mask now (for example 15 L/min), without waiting for the SpO2 to fall
Two large-bore IV cannulae with bloods: group and crossmatch, FBC, coagulation with fibrinogen, and venous gas with lactate
Warmed IV crystalloid, limited in volume, while blood is arranged; lies her flat and keeps her temperature at 36 °C or above

check.x: Treats tone first: fundal massage with clot expulsion, and empties the bladder with an indwelling catheter.

Names uterotonics in order with routes, checking contraindications (doses per local protocol): oxytocin IM already given, a further oxytocin dose by slow IV injection and an oxytocin infusion, ergometrine IM (no hypertension), then carboprost IM (no asthma) or misoprostol if bleeding continues.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, as soon as possible and within 3 hours of birth, with a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes.
Performs bimanual uterine compression while bleeding continues and definitive care is arranged.
Activates the massive transfusion protocol and calls theatre now, by 1,500 mL at the latest.
Calls with key information only: to blood bank ("Primary PPH, A-positive, MTP, delivery suite room 1"), and to the theatre manager rather than reception.
Answers her questions honestly and simply: the team is controlling the bleeding; removing the womb is a last resort only if other measures fail; she can hold her baby once she is stable.
Explains that the early discharge is cancelled and she will stay on monitored observations, with a repeat Hb and an iron plan, a review of her clot risk and a debrief.
Safety netting
Discharge only when bleeding has settled, the uterus is firm, pulse is under 100, systolic BP is above 100 mmHg without dizziness on standing, and she is passing urine.

Tells her to call 000 or come straight back for soaking more than one pad an hour, clots larger than a golf ball, fever of 38 °C or above, smelly discharge, dizziness or fainting, palpitations or breathlessness, or calf pain or swelling.
Arranges follow-up: FBC and ferritin, GP and midwife review, and a plan to give birth in a hospital with blood transfusion available in any future pregnancy.

part2.lead: Here are her observations on arrival and on reassessment 5 minutes later while the bleeding continued, her first blood results and a venous blood gas.

handover.label: Observations on arrival and reassessment 5 minutes later
handover.result: Blood loss measured by weighing pads and linen. Reassessed at 14:40 while the bleeding continued.
handover.model:
Read: on arrival HR 135, BP 100/60, RR 26, SpO2 95% on room air, CRT 4 seconds, temperature 36.4 °C, alert, BGL 5.6, with about 1,000 mL lost: shock index 135/100 = 1.35. Five minutes later 1,500 mL lost and still bleeding, HR 140, BP 90/50 (shock index 1.56), RR 28 and SpO2 91% on room air, with the fundus still soft.

Meaning: major primary PPH with haemorrhagic shock that is getting worse despite the first measures. Pregnancy raises the resting heart rate by only 10 to 20, so 135 to 140 is shock, and a fit young woman holds her blood pressure until late: the shock index above 1, the tachypnoea, the slow capillary refill and her dizziness, cold and thirst show the compromise before the BP falls. A soft fundus with a complete placenta and only a graze points to atony (Tone), helped by the precipitate labour, the full bladder and no breastfeeding; Trauma and Tissue are unlikely on the examination, and Thrombin is checked with the bloods.

What it changes: escalate now. Obstetric registrar or consultant and anaesthetist; high-flow oxygen by face mask at 15 L/min; activate the massive transfusion protocol and call theatre, as she has reached 1,500 mL; bimanual compression while uterotonics and tranexamic acid are given; and repeat observations at least every 5 minutes.

rows.note: Blood loss about 1,000 mL by weighed pads and still bleeding
Blood loss now 1,500 mL and still bleeding; fundus still soft; anxious

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: First bloods, taken when the first cannula was sited.
handover.model:
Read: Hb 96 g/L against a booking 124, below the 100 g/L that defines anaemia after birth; white cells 15.8, flagged high against the lab's non-pregnant range but usual just after labour (up to about 17 in late pregnancy and higher in labour); platelets 168, INR 1.1 and APTT 27 normal; fibrinogen 2.3 g/L, inside the non-pregnant range but low for term, when it is usually 4 to 6; group A positive with a negative antibody screen.

Meaning: haemoglobin falls late, so this early Hb badly underestimates a 1,000 to 1,500 mL loss. Fibrinogen is the earliest marker of severity: a level near or below 2 g/L predicts progression to severe PPH. The normal INR, APTT and platelets show no established coagulopathy yet, but it will come with ongoing loss and dilution.

What it changes: transfuse on the clinical picture and the ongoing loss, not on this Hb, through the massive transfusion protocol (group-specific blood is quick as her group is known); give cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L and platelets above 50; limit crystalloid; repeat FBC, coagulation and fibrinogen (or viscoelastic testing) while she bleeds.

rows.v: A RhD positive, antibody screen negative; crossmatch in progress

handover.label: Venous blood gas
handover.result: Venous sample, taken with the first bloods. Ranges are for non-pregnant adults; in late pregnancy and the first days after birth the pCO2 and bicarbonate run lower (a compensated respiratory alkalosis).
handover.model:
Read: venous pH 7.30 (acidaemia) with bicarbonate 16 and base excess -9 (a metabolic acidosis) and lactate 5.2 mmol/L (high): a lactic acidosis. The low pCO2 of 34 is partial respiratory compensation on top of the lower pCO2 of pregnancy. Glucose, potassium and ionised calcium are normal.

Meaning: tissue hypoperfusion from haemorrhagic shock, confirming what the observations show; acidosis also worsens bleeding (with hypothermia and coagulopathy, the lethal triad).

What it changes: stop the bleeding and restore perfusion with blood products rather than more crystalloid; keep her warm (36 °C or above) and the ionised calcium above 1.1 mmol/L as blood is given; repeat the gas and lactate to judge whether resuscitation is working.

ask: You are now calling the obstetric registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of this patient, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of this patient now, here on the birth suite.

The bleeding is now slowing: total loss 1,800 mL, HR 110, BP 100/62, and she is alert. She asks you: "Am I going to die? Will I need my womb taken out? Am I still going home today?" What would you tell her, and what follow-up would you arrange?
part2.patient: In Part 2, once the candidate is told the bleeding is slowing, the patient asks: "Am I going to die?" "Will I need my womb taken out?" "Am I still going home today?" "Can I still hold my baby?" "What should I look out for later?"
expect:
• Identify: junior doctor, birth suite room 1. Patient is a 24-year-old G2P2, 40 minutes after a vaginal birth at 39 weeks.
  • Situation: major primary PPH, 1,500 mL lost and still bleeding, with worsening shock. I need you now.
  • Background: 2-hour precipitate labour; oxytocin 10 units IM given; placenta and membranes complete; graze only; full bladder; formula feeding; no hypertension or asthma; booking Hb 124; A-positive, antibody screen negative.
  • Assessment: shock index has gone from 1.35 to 1.56 (HR 140, BP 90/50, SpO2 91%); fundus is soft, so this is atony. Hb 96 underestimates the loss. Fibrinogen 2.3 is low for term. INR and platelets are normal. Lactate 5.2 and BE -9 show hypoperfusion.
  • Recommendation: please attend now. The anaesthetist has been called and the MTP is activated. Theatre has been called and tranexamic acid and uterotonics are under way.

Most likely: major primary PPH from uterine atony (Tone), with haemorrhagic shock.

  • For it: the fundus is soft, boggy and above the umbilicus. Risk factors are the precipitate labour, a full bladder and no breastfeeding. Bleeding became heavy after the placenta was delivered.

Differentials (4 Ts):

  • Trauma (cervical or vaginal tear, haematoma, rupture, inversion): against it, inspection shows only a graze and the fundus is palpable.
  • Tissue (retained placenta or membranes): against it, both were checked complete.
  • Thrombin (coagulopathy): INR, APTT and platelets are normal, but fibrinogen 2.3 is low for term. Coagulopathy can develop with ongoing loss and dilution.

1. Help and roles: obstetric registrar or consultant, anaesthetist and senior midwife; a scribe keeps a T-sheet.
  2. Resuscitation: oxygen by face mask at 15 L/min; lie her flat and keep her warm. Two large-bore cannulae; send crossmatch, FBC, coagulation with fibrinogen and a venous gas. Give limited warmed crystalloid.
  3. Tone: fundal massage, expel clots and insert an indwelling catheter.
  4. Uterotonics (local protocol): oxytocin 5 units slow IV, then an infusion. Ergometrine 250 micrograms IM (no hypertension). Carboprost 250 micrograms IM every 15 minutes, maximum 8 doses (no asthma), or misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingual.
  5. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, within 3 hours of birth. Repeat 1 g if still bleeding after 30 minutes.
  6. Bimanual compression.
  7. MTP and theatre now (1,500 mL reached). Brief calls: blood bank ("Primary PPH, A-positive, MTP, delivery suite room 1") and the theatre manager.
  8. Keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L, platelets above 50 and temperature at 36 °C or above. Repeat the gas and fibrinogen.

• Honest answers: the bleeding is slowing and the team is in control. Removing the womb is a last resort, only if other measures fail. She can hold her baby once she is stable.
  • Discharge is cancelled: she stays on monitored observations. She gets a repeat Hb with an iron plan, a clot-risk (VTE) review and a debrief.
  • She can go home when: bleeding has settled, the uterus is firm, pulse is under 100, systolic BP is above 100 with no dizziness on standing, and she is passing urine.
  • Call 000 or come straight back for: soaking more than one pad an hour, clots bigger than a golf ball, fever of 38 °C or above, smelly discharge, dizziness or fainting, palpitations or breathlessness, or calf pain or swelling.
  • Follow-up: FBC and ferritin, GP and midwife review. In any future pregnancy she should give birth in a hospital with blood transfusion available.
